items.question: She's ___ nurse at the local hospital.
explanations: Jobs take a/an, not 'one'. 'One nurse' stresses a number nobody asked about.
'The one' can't introduce a job.
Correct! A job: 'a nurse'. 'Nurse' starts with a consonant sound, so 'a'.
'Nurse' starts with a consonant sound, so 'a', not 'an'.

items.question: He's ___ engineer at a tech company.
explanations: 'Engineer' starts with a vowel sound (/e/), so the article is 'an'.
'The one' can't introduce a job.
Jobs take a/an, not 'one'.
Correct! A job, and 'engineer' starts with a vowel sound: 'an engineer'.

items.question: Two pizzas? — No, just ___ pizza, please.
explanations: Here the number matters ('two?' → 'just one'), so we use 'one', not 'a'.
Correct! The number is the point (one, not two), so we use 'one'.
'The one' points to a specific pizza, not to the number.
'An' is only for vowel sounds, and 'pizza' starts with a consonant sound.

items.question: ___ day I'll visit Japan. (some time in the future)
explanations: Correct! 'One day' is a fixed phrase for an unspecified future time.
'A day' doesn't mean 'at some time in the future'. The fixed phrase is 'one day'.
'An day' is wrong: 'day' starts with a consonant sound.
'The one day' changes the meaning.

items.question: There are two jackets. I'll take the black ___ .
explanations: Correct! 'One' replaces the noun: 'the black one' = 'the black jacket'.
'A' needs a noun after it. It can't replace 'jacket'.
'An' needs a noun after it. It can't replace 'jacket'.
'It' can't follow an adjective: 'the black it' is wrong.

items.question: I saw ___ amazing film last night.
explanations: 'Amazing' starts with a vowel sound (/ə/), so 'an', not 'a'.
'One amazing film' stresses the number, but nobody asked how many.
'The one' points to a film we both know. This is the first mention.
Correct! First mention, and 'amazing' starts with a vowel sound: 'an amazing film'.

items.question: Only ___ student passed the exam — everyone else failed.
explanations: 'A student' just names the noun and doesn't stress 'only one'.
Correct! 'Only' + contrast with 'everyone else' makes the number matter: 'one student'.
'An' is for vowel sounds, and 'student' starts with a consonant sound.
'The one student' points to someone specific. It isn't about the number.

items.question: Which sentence is correct?
explanations: Jobs take a/an. 'One doctor' wrongly stresses the number.
A job needs a/an before it: 'a doctor'. Without an article the sentence is incorrect.
Correct! Jobs take a/an: 'a doctor'.
'Doctor' starts with a consonant sound, so 'a', not 'an'.

items.question: Which sentence uses 'one' as a pronoun?
explanations: Here 'one' is a number before a noun (brother).
This is the fixed pattern 'one of + plural', not a pronoun replacing a noun.
This is the fixed phrase 'one day'.
Correct! 'One' stands instead of a noun (the red shirt, the red car…) and has no noun after it.

items.question: When do you use 'one' instead of 'a/an'?
options: When the number matters, in fixed phrases, or to replace a noun.
explanations: Most singular nouns just take a/an.
Jobs take a/an, not 'one'.
Correct! Number, fixed phrases (one day, one of…) and the pronoun use.
'One' isn't limited to questions.

items.question: I'd like ___ coffee, not two.
items.explanation: 'Not two' makes the number the point, so we use 'one'.

common.why: 'A coffee' only names the drink. The contrast with 'two' needs 'one'.

items.question: ___ day I'll travel the world. (= at some time in the future; fixed phrase)
items.hint: Type the missing word, or the whole sentence.
answers: One day I will travel the world
One day I'll travel the world
items.explanation: 'One day' is the fixed phrase for an unspecified time in the future.

common.why: 'A day' doesn't mean 'some time in the future'. Use the fixed phrase 'one day'.
